title: HSBC and Citi Turn Bullish on India as Foreign Inflows Head for a Record Week
excerpt: HSBC upgraded India to overweight and Citi raised its end-2027 Nifty target to 28,000 after overseas funds bought $3.6 billion of shares in four days.
body:
• HSBC has upgraded Indian equities to overweight from neutral and Citi has raised its Nifty 50 target to 28,000 for end-2027, nearly 8% higher than its previous target — both are brokerage estimates, not outcomes.
  • Overseas funds bought a net $3.6 billion of Indian shares in the four days through Thursday, with provisional data showing another $1.5 billion on Friday, putting the week on course for a record inflow.
  • The benchmark is up nearly 8% this month, its strongest month since July 2022, after foreign investors spent much of two years cutting India exposure.
  • On Monday the Sensex closed at 81,106.65, up 107.25 points, and the Nifty at 25,044.65, up 58.25 points, after recovering about 1% from the day's low.

Global brokerages are turning bullish on Indian equities again, as the market's sharpest rally in more than four years draws record foreign money back in. HSBC lifted Indian equities to overweight from neutral, citing resilient earnings and more reasonable valuations, while Citi raised its 12-month Nifty 50 target by nearly 8% to 28,000, pointing to improving profit growth and lower oil prices, The Hindu BusinessLine reported, citing Bloomberg.

What the brokerages are actually saying

HSBC's strategists, including Herald van der Linde, wrote that India offers diversification and low volatility in Asian markets dominated by AI stocks, and said they favour banks, industrials, consumer discretionary companies, insurers and hospitals. Citi's analysts, including Surendra Goyal and Vijit Jain, expect Nifty earnings to grow about 15%-16% annually across fiscal 2026-2028, and estimate that a $10 decline in oil prices could lift Nifty earnings per share by about 2%. These are forecasts: the target and the earnings path are Citi's estimates, and the HSBC rating is a recommendation, not a result.

"India offers diversification and low volatility in Asian markets dominated by AI stocks."

— HSBC strategists including Herald van der Linde, via Bloomberg

The flows behind the calls

The upgrades follow the money. Overseas funds bought a net $3.6 billion of local shares in the four days through Thursday, on course for their biggest-ever weekly inflow, with provisional data showing another $1.5 billion of purchases on Friday. Citi sees room for more: a percentage-point increase in active fund allocations to India could generate about $12 billion of inflows, its analysts estimate, after AI crowded out almost everything else in portfolios. The benchmark index is up nearly 8% this month, the most since July 2022.

Monday's trade

Local stocks slipped during Monday's session before recovering. The Sensex closed at 81,106.65, up 107.25 points or 0.13%, and the Nifty 50 at 25,044.65, up 58.25 points or 0.23%, after both recovered around 1% from the day's low, according to market reporting of the session. The same reporting put November's net FII buying so far at Rs 45,970 crore and linked the turn in foreign sentiment to the AI sell-off in the US, South Korea, Taiwan and Japan.

Why the reversal matters

Foreign investors spent much of the past two years cutting exposure to India while chasing AI-driven gains elsewhere in Asia and the US, which left positioning light. That is the mechanical core of the bullish case: if earnings hold near the brokerages' estimates and crude stays soft, even a partial rebuilding of foreign allocations is a large flow. If earnings disappoint, the same targets will be revised back down — they are a measure of sentiment turning, not a promise.
